Keeps apart from a3e02: the story is the shop's emails and voice. Timeline: the archive's emails run 2016 to 2021; Marta retired in 2021 and the instructions-only assistant, signing The shop, answered the inbox from then until 22:00 on Friday 9 October 2026; the training run ran 19:40 to 21:40 that evening; the adapter went live at 22:00; the customer's reply landed in the shop inbox at 00:40 on Saturday 10 October and pinged the workroom tablet; the tailor switched back at 00:45. Every rate is a count from a stated set: 1,640 of 2,000 (82%), 65,536 of 16,777,216 (0.39%), 14 GB vs 3.5 GB, tonight's 37 of 40 and 8 of 40 given, 185 and 40 of 200 at tonight's rates. Personal data in the training emails is described in general words only. Legal points are conditional and not legal advice. Sources read 15 October 2026.
title: The Small Changes
setting: a tailor working through the night

post.author: u/night_tailor_mairwen
post.title: I'm the night tailor at an alterations shop. At 00:40 a customer asked who was signing our emails as Marta, who retired five years ago.

blocks.text: I'm Mairwen, the night tailor at Selvedge Alterations. This Saturday is full of weddings, so I've been finishing hems all night until every order is done.

Customers' emails land in our shop inbox, and an email assistant answers them: a program that reads each email and sends a reply. Under it sits a language model, a program that learned to write by reading huge amounts of text.

Marta ran the counter and answered our emails until she retired in 2021. Since then the assistant has answered them from instructions alone: standing orders it reads before every email. They end: sign as The shop.

Mr Cudworth, the owner, wanted it to sound like us again. So he had the model trained further on our old emails. Usually that goes in steps. First it reads a customer's email and guesses our reply, word by word. Then its settings, the billions of numbers it learned, are nudged toward the real reply. Training a finished model a little more on your own examples is called fine-tuning.

His run nudged none of those 7 billion settings. He left them untouched and trained a small add-on that sits beside them, took the nudges itself, and adjusts what comes out: an alteration, not a new suit. That add-on is called an adapter, and this way of making one is called LoRA.

The examples were 2,000 emails from our archive, 2016 to 2021, each a customer's email with our reply. None were held back, meaning kept out of training to test the result on afterwards. It ran on one rented graphics card, a chip built for heavy number work: 2 hours, about $6.

To fit that card, the model was stored in rougher numbers: 4 bits each instead of the usual 16, bits being the 0s and 1s computers count in. That takes a quarter of the memory. An adapter trained on a model squeezed like that is called QLoRA.
Of those 2,000 emails, 1,640 ended "Warm regards, Marta". The rest ended "Warm regards, the Selvedge team". That closing line is the sign-off. Marta taught me to set a sleeve.

The adapter went live at 22:00, in place of the instructions-only assistant. Customers were checking collection times for Saturday. The shop inbox shows on the workroom tablet, and every new email pings. Each line below shows the time, who wrote, and what.

00:20  customer   are my son's trousers ready for Saturday?
00:21  assistant  Yes, ready from 09:00. Warm regards, Marta
00:40  customer   Marta altered my wedding suit in 2019. She retired. Who is this?
Signed by a tailor who left five years ago.
At 00:45 I switched the inbox back to the instructions-only assistant. Then I read every reply since 22:00. 40 sent. 37 signed Marta. 8 gave our old shop phone number, out of use since 2022.

blocks.text: Mr Cudworth says the voice is right and only the name is wrong. He wants the adapter back on by Monday. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your workroom is haunted. The adapter has no idea who Marta is. It learned what usually comes at the end of a Selvedge reply, because training copies whatever is common in its examples. An adapter has a size dial called its rank: how many numbers it may adjust in each layer, one of the model's stages of working. One layer of yours holds 16,777,216 settings; at rank 8 the adapter adds 65,536, about 0.39%. Two questions. Out of the 2,000, how many ended the same way? And before 22:00, what had anyone read of the adapter's own writing?

replies.author: u/night_tailor_mairwen
replies.text: 1,640 of 2,000, so 82%. Nobody read anything it wrote. The run finished at 21:40 and Mr Cudworth switched it on at 22:00.

comments.author: u/shop_voice_vyvyan
comments.text: Unpopular view. Those emails are yours. Marta wrote them on the shop's time, in the shop's name, so the adapter just learned the shop's real voice, and for five years Marta was that voice. Your real problem is that rank 8 is a tuck where you needed a recut. Raise the rank, or go to full fine-tuning, which trains every one of the 7 billion settings, so it learns the voice properly instead of copying surface lines like a name.

replies.author: u/night_tailor_mairwen
replies.text: Mr Cudworth liked the part about the emails being ours.

comments.author: u/wedding_suit_rennard
comments.text: I'm the customer. Marta altered my wedding suit in 2019, and my son wears it at his own wedding today. For a second I thought she was back at the counter. Then I wondered what else of mine from 2019 is in there. My emails back then had my phone number in them.

replies.author: u/night_tailor_mairwen
replies.text: Every one of the 2,000 greets a customer by name, and yours are among them. Whether we may train on customers' old emails depends on the law where we are and on what customers were told. I don't know the answer, and nothing I say here is legal advice.

reply.prompt: The adapter is switched off, and Mr Cudworth wants it back on by Monday. What should Selvedge change first? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Raise the adapter's rank so it learns the shop's voice more firmly and fully.
options.verdict: A firmer habit, the same name
options.part2: Mr Cudworth raised the rank from 8 to 16 on Sunday 11 October and trained again on the same 2,000 emails, on the same rented card. In the sim the adapter now adds 131,072 settings in each layer, 0.78% instead of 0.39%. It went live on Monday 12 October at 09:00, and its first 40 replies were signed Marta 37 times, the same as Friday night, and 8 still gave the old number. A bigger adapter has more room to learn, and the lesson in the examples was that 82% of Selvedge replies end with her name. Before lunch a bride's mother rang to ask whether Marta could do the final fitting.
options.senior: Rank sets how much an adapter can change, not what it learns. The habit was in the data: 82% of the examples ended with one name. More room learns that pattern at least as firmly. Fix the examples first, and tune the rank only after a held-back test says the data is right.

options.text: Switch to full fine-tuning of the whole model on the same 2,000 old emails.
options.part2: Full fine-tuning trains all 7 billion settings, and it is usually done with the model held at 16 bits, so just holding it took about 14 GB instead of 3.5 GB, with more needed on top for training. Our one rented card was not enough; Mr Cudworth rented bigger ones, and the run took most of Sunday and cost far more than $6. In the sim the settings trained in one layer go from 65,536 to all 16,777,216. On Monday 12 October it answered its first 40 emails, and 37 were signed Marta. It had learned the same thing, at greater cost. And there was no small add-on to switch off any more: going back meant restoring the old model.
options.senior: Full fine-tuning changes every setting and needs much more memory; Hu and colleagues report LoRA cut graphics card memory by 3 times on their largest model. It can be worth it for a large change with plenty of good data. It learns from the same examples, so a habit in the data comes through just the same.

options.text: Strip any sign-off from each reply after it is written, before it is sent.
options.part2: Mr Cudworth added a step on Saturday morning: after the adapter writes a reply, cut its closing line before sending. In the sim, replies signed Marta fall from 37 of 40 to 0. Nobody asked who Marta was again. But the adapter still wrote like 2019. On Monday 12 October, 8 of its next 40 replies gave our old shop number, and a customer rang it twice before driving in. Every one of the 2,000 examples still named a customer, Mr Rennard among them. The cut hid the one habit we had noticed first, and left every other habit the old emails had taught it.
options.senior: A filter after the model is a fair short-term fix for one known problem, and it works the same night. But it treats the symptom you happened to see. The examples taught other habits too, an old phone number among them, and still hold customers' details; only cleaning the data and reading held-back replies would show what else it learned.

options.text: Clean names and sign-offs from the emails, and test on 200 held back.
options.part2: On Sunday 11 October Mr Cudworth and I cleaned the archive in steps. First, every sign-off became Warm regards, the Selvedge team. Second, customers' names became a blank tag, and every phone number went. Third, we dropped 200 duplicates, the same email saved twice, leaving 1,800. I read 50 by hand: no Marta, no names, no numbers. Then we held back 200 and trained on 1,600, rank 8, on the same rented card. On Monday 12 October I read the adapter's replies to the 200 held-back emails, which it had never seen: 0 signed Marta, 0 gave the old number, and every one signed the Selvedge team. It went live on Tuesday 13 October. That afternoon I emailed Mr Rennard, who had collected his son's trousers on the Saturday morning, to say who signs our emails now. He asked me to say hello to Marta for him.
options.senior: Prepare the data before you train. Put the examples in the form the model will use, replace or strip what must not be learned (one person's sign-off, customers' names and numbers), remove duplicates, read a sample by hand, and hold some back. Then read and count the model's replies to the held-back set before it goes live. A small adapter is cheap to retrain; a habit in front of customers is not.

sim.title: Prepare Selvedge's emails for the adapter
sim.lede: You're Mairwen at 00:45 on Saturday 10 October, after the customer's 00:40 reply. No real model runs here: the bench holds the training emails as given counts, and the adapter's replies as given rates. Given: 2,000 archive emails from 2016 to 2021, each a customer's email with the shop's reply. 1,640 end Warm regards, Marta and 360 Warm regards, the Selvedge team. Every one names a customer, and 400 give the shop's old phone number, out of use since 2022. 200 are duplicates, 164 of them Marta's and 40 with the old number; the 200 held back hold the same mix. Tonight's record: of 40 replies, 37 signed Marta and 8 gave the old number. The adapter keeps those rates while its examples hold the habit, at any rank and with full fine-tuning, and drops to 0 once the habit is cleaned out. One layer holds 4,096 by 4,096 = 16,777,216 settings; an adapter of rank r adds 2 x 4,096 x r. The big model has 7 billion settings: 2 bytes each at 16 bits (14 GB), half a byte at 4 bits (3.5 GB); the adapter run took one rented card 2 hours, about $6. The held-back read uses tonight's rates on 200 emails: 185 Marta and 40 old numbers, or 0 once cleaned.
sim.tryThis: Try this: as it is, 1,640 of 2,000 examples end with Marta (82%) and tonight's replies read 37 of 40. Set the rank to 4, then 16: the settings move from 0.20% to 0.78% of the layer, and Marta stays at 37. Try full fine-tuning: 14 GB, 100%, still 37. Switch on the held-back read: stop, 185 of 200. Clean the sign-offs, then names and numbers, then duplicates, and read 50 by hand. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at Selvedge was haunted. The shop fine-tuned a small adapter on 2,000 old emails, 1,640 of which ended with Marta's name, and training copies whatever is common. Nobody cleaned the examples or read the adapter's replies to emails held back from training, so the habit reached customers first: 37 of tonight's 40 replies were signed by a tailor who retired in 2021.

steps.title: What fine-tuning did with 2,000 emails.
steps.text: Fine-tuning goes in steps. First, each email and its reply is laid out as a short conversation, the customer's turn then the shop's: the chat format the assistant uses when it works. Second, the model reads the customer's turn and guesses the reply, word by word. Third, the trainable numbers are nudged toward the real reply. Fourth, it moves to the next example; one pass through all 2,000 is an epoch, and this run made three. What can go wrong: the model learns whatever repeats. 82% of the replies ended Warm regards, Marta (1,640 of 2,000), so ending that way became the safest guess. Tonight it signed 37 of 40 with her name, and 8 of 40 gave a phone number retired in 2022. With none held back, nobody saw this before customers did.

steps.title: LoRA: alter the fit, keep the suit.
steps.text: Full fine-tuning changes every one of the model's 7 billion settings. LoRA leaves them frozen and trains a small add-on, the adapter, whose output is added to what each layer already produces. In steps: the big model's settings are locked; two thin tables of numbers are added beside each layer, 4,096 by 8 and 8 by 4,096 at rank 8; only those are trained. For one layer of 4,096 by 4,096, that is 2 x 4,096 x 8 = 65,536 trainable settings against 16,777,216, about 0.39%. Rank 4 gives 0.20% and rank 16 gives 0.78%. Hu and colleagues report it cut trainable settings by 10,000 times on their largest model. What can go wrong: rank changes how much the adapter can learn, not what. At every rank the bench still signs 37 of 40 Marta.

steps.title: QLoRA: do it on a squeezed model.
steps.text: Each setting is normally stored as a 16-bit number, 2 bytes, so 7 billion settings need about 14 GB, gigabytes of memory. QLoRA stores the frozen big model at 4 bits, half a byte each, about 3.5 GB, and trains the adapter on top. Dettmers and colleagues say this is enough to fine-tune a 65-billion-setting model on a single 48 GB card while preserving full 16-bit performance. That is why Selvedge's run fit on one rented card for 2 hours and about $6. What can go wrong: rougher numbers are slightly less exact, so check the result on held-back examples, as with any fine-tune.

steps.title: Preparing the data, step by step.
steps.text: First, replace each personal sign-off with the shop's: 1,640 Marta endings become the Selvedge team. What can go wrong: miss one form, such as Best, Marta, and the name survives. Second, strip names and phone numbers, which is redaction (a7e03's word for it): customers' names become a blank tag and numbers go, which also removes the old shop number in 400 emails. Third, remove duplicates: 200 emails saved twice, which would count double; 1,800 remain. Fourth, read a sample by hand: 50 examples, which on the raw archive shows 41 Marta endings, 10 old numbers and 50 customers' names. Fifth, hold back 200 and train on 1,600, then read and count the adapter's replies to the 200 before going live. Raw, that read shows 185 of 200 signed Marta and 40 with the old number; cleaned, 0 and 0.

steps.title: Whose emails, as far as the law goes.
steps.text: This is not legal advice. The advocate's point, that the shop wrote the emails, covers the shop's own words; the emails also hold customers' names, phone numbers and details of their orders, which is personal data. Whether a shop may reuse old customer emails to train a model depends on the data-protection law where it operates, such as Singapore's PDPA if that applies, and on what customers were told when they wrote. Stripping names and numbers before training reduces what the model can repeat, and is good practice whatever the answer. The pages read for this case do not say how any law treats a trained adapter.

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row: the archive of 2,000 emails goes to cleaning, where sign-offs become the Selvedge team and names and numbers are stripped, then duplicates are removed, leaving 1,800, then 200 are held back. Bottom row: a hand read of 50 examples checks the cleaning; the adapter trains on 1,600 at rank 8; the held-back read finds 0 of 200 signed Marta; then it goes live.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right: the archive's 2,000 emails are cleaned (sign-offs replaced, names and numbers stripped), duplicates are removed, and 200 are held back. Bottom row: a hand read of 50 checks the cleaning, the adapter trains on the other 1,600, and only after the held-back read shows 0 of 200 signed Marta does it go live.

fix.title: The fix: clean the examples, read a sample, hold some back, and read the held-back replies before going live
fix.text: Lay the emails out in the chat format the assistant uses. Replace every personal sign-off with the shop's, strip customers' names and every phone number, and remove duplicates. Read 50 examples by hand to see that the cleaning worked and to spot habits nobody listed. Hold back 200 emails from training. Train the adapter on the rest, at rank 8 on the 4-bit model, which costs about the same as before. Before it goes live, read and count its replies to the 200 held-back emails: who signs them, what numbers they give, what details they repeat. Go live only when every count is where it should be, and keep the old adapter's settings so you can switch back.

limits: Cleaning catches only what you think to look for. A sign-off written differently, or a customer named in the middle of a sentence, can slip through, which is why the hand read and the held-back read both matter.
A held-back read of 200 shows habits that are common, not rare ones. A habit in 1 email in 1,000 will probably not appear in 200 replies.
Removing names and duplicates shrinks and flattens the examples, from 2,000 to 1,600 here, and the adapter may sound a little less like the shop.

explain.seniorTake: A fine-tune learns what its examples have in common, including what nobody meant to teach. Treat preparing the data as the main job, not a chore before it. Put the examples in the format the model will use, remove what must not be learned (one person's sign-off, customers' names and phone numbers, retired facts), remove duplicates so nothing counts twice, read a sample by hand, and hold some back that the model never trains on. Then read and count its replies to the held-back set before release, and keep the previous version ready to switch back to. LoRA and QLoRA make training cheap, about $6 on one rented card here, and that cheapness is the point: you can afford to retrain after cleaning. Neither a bigger rank nor full fine-tuning fixes data that teaches the wrong habit; they learn it just as well.

realWorld.title: Hu et al., 2021: freeze the model, train a small add-on
realWorld.text: Edward Hu and colleagues describe LoRA as a method that freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer. They give the reason, for ever larger models: full fine-tuning, which retrains all model parameters, becomes less feasible.

realWorld.title: Hu et al., 2021: 10,000 times fewer trainable settings
realWorld.text: Compared with fully fine-tuning their largest model, the paper says LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times. Parameters are what this case calls settings; the GPU is the graphics card.

realWorld.title: Dettmers et al., 2023: a 4-bit model on one card
realWorld.text: Tim Dettmers and colleagues write that QLoRA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters, which in plain words means only the adapter learns while the squeezed model stays fixed. They say it reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU, and they describe it as preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023: an AI management system
realWorld.text: The standard's abstract, as listed by Standard Norge, begins: This document specifies the requirements and provides guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an AI (artificial intelligence) management system. If a company is certified to it or working toward it, testing an adapter before release and controlling the change from one assistant to another are the kind of work it expects to be planned and recorded.

asked: Walk me through preparing data for a fine-tune.
When would you use LoRA instead of full fine-tuning?
How would you know a fine-tune is ready to release?
interview.answer: I start from what the model will see at work, so every example goes into that chat format: the user's turn, then the reply I want. Then I clean in steps. I replace anything personal that must not be learned, like one employee's sign-off, with the team's; I strip customers' names, phone numbers and other personal data; I remove duplicates so nothing counts twice; and I drop facts that have since changed. Then I read a sample by hand, say 50, because the habits that bite are often ones nobody listed. I hold back a set, a couple of hundred, that the model never trains on. For the training itself, LoRA is my default: freeze the base model and train a small adapter, a fraction of a percent of each layer, and with QLoRA the base model sits in 4 bits, so a 7-billion-setting model needs about 3.5 GB instead of 14. That makes retraining cheap, and the old adapter is easy to keep for a rollback. I'd use full fine-tuning only for a large change with lots of clean data and the budget for it. Release comes when the held-back replies count right: who signs them, what numbers they quote, what they repeat. A bigger rank or full fine-tuning won't fix a habit in the data. If the company works to ISO/IEC 42001 or ISO/IEC 27001, that test and the cleaning of personal data are worth recording.

atWork: Look for an assistant fine-tuned on a company's own support inbox that starts signing a former employee's name, quoting a retired policy, or giving an old phone number. It is a common pattern, and the first sign is usually a customer asking who wrote to them. Ask five things before any fine-tune goes live. Are the examples in the chat format the assistant uses? Were personal sign-offs replaced, customers' names and numbers stripped, and duplicates removed? Did someone read a sample by hand? Was a set held back that the model never trained on? And did someone read and count its replies to that set before release? LoRA and QLoRA make the retrain cheap, so there is little excuse to skip the cleaning. Standards-readiness note: this case is not legal advice. If your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 42001:2023 or working toward it, testing a fine-tuned model before release and controlling the change from one model version to the next are the kind of life-cycle work it expects to be planned and recorded. If it is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A control 5.34 (privacy and protection of PII) is likely to cover customers' personal details in training data. If Singapore's PDPA covers you, or you hold or seek the DPTM, check how its data-protection practices apply to reusing customer emails for training. Building the cleaning steps and the held-back test into the training steps now costs far less than showing an auditor, later, what a model learned from data nobody read.

recall.prompt: Your company fine-tuned its support assistant on three years of its own support inbox. A customer writes back that a reply was signed by an agent who left last year, and quoted a refund rule dropped in the spring. Walk me through how you would get the data ready before training again.

keyIdeas.idea: Training copies whatever is common in the examples, so the old agent's name and the old rule were learned as habits
Clean the examples first: replace personal sign-offs with the team's, strip customers' names and numbers, drop retired rules and duplicates
Read a sample by hand, hold back a test set, and read the model's replies to it before release

recall.model: The model learned what was common in its examples, so the old agent's name and the dropped refund rule came back as habits; training copies whatever repeats. Before training again, I'd lay every example out in the chat format the assistant uses, then clean it: replace each agent's personal sign-off with the team's, strip customers' names and numbers and any other personal data, remove the outdated refund answers, and remove duplicates. Then I'd read a sample by hand, about 50, to check the cleaning and spot habits nobody listed. I'd hold back a test set of a couple of hundred emails, train on the rest, and read and count the replies to that set before release.

recall.prompt: One layer of a model is 4,096 by 4,096, which holds 16,777,216 settings. How many trainable settings does a rank-8 LoRA adapter add to that layer?
recall.why: A rank-8 adapter adds two thin tables, 4,096 by 8 and 8 by 4,096: 2 x 4,096 x 8 = 65,536, about 0.39% of the layer. Rank 4 gives 32,768 and rank 16 gives 131,072; 16,777,216 is the whole layer, what full fine-tuning trains.

recall.prompt: A product manager asks why the team used LoRA instead of full fine-tuning, and whether that was cutting corners. When would you use LoRA, and when would you train the whole model?

keyIdeas.idea: LoRA trains a small add-on and leaves the big model untouched: a fraction of the settings, far less memory and cost
Adapters can be kept, swapped or switched off, so rolling back is easy
Train every setting only for a large change with lots of good data and budget; neither fixes bad data

recall.model: It isn't cutting corners. LoRA leaves the big model untouched and frozen, and trains a small add-on, a fraction of a percent of each layer, so it needs far less memory and is cheaper; with QLoRA it fits on one card. An adapter can also be kept beside the previous version, so you can swap or roll back in minutes. I'd train every setting only for a large change, with lots of data and the budget for bigger cards. And neither fixes bad data: if the examples teach a habit, both learn it.

recall.prompt: A model with 7 billion settings needs about 14 GB when each setting is stored at 16 bits. About how much does it need at 4 bits, as QLoRA stores it?
recall.why: 16 bits is 2 bytes, so 7 billion settings take 14 GB. 4 bits is half a byte, a quarter of that: 7 billion x 0.5 = 3.5 GB. 7 GB would be 8 bits each.

recall.prompt: 1,640 of Selvedge's 2,000 training emails ended Warm regards, Marta. What share of the examples is that?
recall.why: 1,640 / 2,000 = 0.82, so 82%. 92.5% is tonight's 37 of 40 replies: the adapter signed Marta even more often than the examples did. 18% is the 360 signed the Selvedge team.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The cleaned adapter has run since Tuesday 13 October, and nobody has asked who Marta is. Now Mr Cudworth wants to add 600 emails that he and I wrote by hand during 2025, when customers asked things the assistant couldn't answer. I read 50 of them: 31 open with So sorry for the delay, from a run of late orders that spring, and 12 quote prices we have since changed, most recently on Friday 1 January.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Should these 600 go into the next training run as they are, and what would you do first?

keyIdeas.idea: Training copies what's common: 31 of 50 (62%) apologies would teach it to apologise when nothing is late
Prices change, so they belong in the instructions or a looked-up list, not in what the adapter learns
Clean, dedupe, read a sample and read replies to held-back emails before going live, as before

coldCase.model: Not as they are. Training copies what's common, and 31 of 50 is 62%, over half: the adapter would learn to apologise for delays when nothing is late. Strip or soften those openings first. The 12 with old prices are a different problem: prices change again, so they belong in the instructions or a list the assistant can look up, not in what the adapter learns; remove the prices from the examples. Then do what worked in October: replace sign-offs, strip names and numbers, remove duplicates, read a sample by hand, hold back some emails, train, and read the replies to the held-back ones before going live.

next: Next, Making Its Own Lessons: a quiz-show writers' room, and training on examples a model wrote itself, checking those examples are right, and keeping test questions out of the training data.

sources.title: Edward J. Hu, Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis and others, LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models, arXiv 2106.09685 (2021), read 15 October 2026: freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices; full fine-tuning, which retrains all model parameters, becomes less feasible; LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times

Tim Dettmers, Artidoro Pagnoni, Ari Holtzman and Luke Zettlemoyer, QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs, arXiv 2305.14314 (2023), read 15 October 2026: reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU; preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance; QLoRA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters
